analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare patients privately contract with doctors who don't take Medicare and still use Medicare benefits.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 20, 2026 by Sen. Rand Paul with one cosponsor, it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, a doctor who doesn't accept Medicare's payment rates generally has to opt out of Medicare entirely, and a senior who sees that doctor gives up Medicare coverage for those services. This bill would let any Medicare beneficiary sign a written private contract with a doctor or other clinician for covered care while keeping their Medicare benefits: the patient pays the doctor's private charge, then submits the claim and Medicare pays its usual share. Medicare would pay at the higher 'participating' rate even for doctors who don't participate. The bill removes the usual cap on what a doctor can charge above Medicare's amount and overrides any state law capping those charges.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors who want to keep seeing a doctor that doesn't participate in Medicare without losing their Medicare coverage for that care, and clinicians who want to charge above Medicare's rates while their patients keep Medicare benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors using non-participating doctors, and those doctors

how_it_helps.text: Any Medicare beneficiary could sign a written contract with any eligible clinician for Medicare-covered care, whether or not that clinician participates in Medicare, and still submit a claim for Medicare payment [S2][S3].

The contract must be signed before care, set the price in advance, hold the patient harmless for later extra charges under that contract, and cannot be signed during an emergency or urgent situation [S3].

Medicare would pay the claim as if the clinician were a participating provider — a higher rate than non-participating providers normally receive — and the patient could negotiate to have the clinician file the claims instead [S2][S3].
People dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid are excluded from these contracts, so the lowest-income beneficiaries cannot be signed into them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Beneficiaries who sign contracts pay the gap between the doctor's private charge and Medicare's payment, which would be uncapped under the bill; the Medicare program would pay participating-level rates to doctors who don't participate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Contracting seniors, who pay any gap above Medicare's payment

drawbacks.text: The bill strips the statutory limit on charges above Medicare's approved amount and preempts any state law capping such charges, so a beneficiary who signs a contract could owe an unlimited amount on top of Medicare's payment [S3].

Because Medicare would still pay its share and doctors could charge extra without penalty, the bill creates a financial incentive for more clinicians to stop participating in Medicare and demand private contracts, which could shrink the standard Medicare network for seniors who don't sign such contracts [S3].

Unless the contract says otherwise, the beneficiary — often an older adult — is responsible for submitting the Medicare and supplemental insurance claims personally, a paperwork burden that falls on the patient [S2][S3].
Patients who sign a contract give up Medicare's limits on what the clinician can charge or be paid, and the contract must state this clearly before they sign [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a senior set on a specific non-participating doctor — say a renowned surgeon — this restores a choice current law takes away, and the advance-written-contract and emergency exclusions are real protections. But the price mechanism cuts the other way: the bill deliberately removes the cap on how much extra a contracted doctor can charge and overrides state charge limits, and Medicare keeps paying its full share. The honest worry is not any single contract but the aggregate effect — a route for more doctors to leave Medicare's fee system and bill seniors the difference, with no ceiling.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on May 20, 2026, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no markup, vote, or floor action so far [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill in the Senate on May 20, 2026, together with one cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over Medicare [S5].
No committee action, vote, or further step has been recorded since the referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened yet; the standard Medicare rules this bill would loosen still apply.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No change yet; current Medicare rules still apply

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republican senators are attached to the bill and no vote has been taken, so no partisan pattern has formed yet.

industries.note: The bill lets clinicians charge patients privately above Medicare's rates with no cap — the limiting-charge rule and state charge caps would not apply — while Medicare still pays its share, even at the higher participating rate. Some patients gain access to doctors they currently can't use Medicare with, but the clinicians' gain comes directly out of the contracting patient's pocket.

Contracted services may generate claims to supplemental plans, and patients would have to submit those claims unless the clinician agrees to do it. The effect on these insurers is secondary and unquantified in the bill materials.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been in the Senate Finance Committee since the day it was introduced, with two sponsors and no committee action. Medicare contracting bills of this kind have historically stalled at this stage; unless the committee schedules a markup, it is likely to die quietly when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
